name: AZD6234

lead: AZD6234 is an experimental long-acting amylin receptor agonist from AstraZeneca for obesity and type 2 diabetes. The payoff people follow it for is greater fullness and fat loss.

Amylin is a satiety hormone released with insulin that acts on the brain and slows glucagon release after meals. The chain is amylin receptor activation, lower appetite, then weight loss and a leaner body. Phase 3 trials were registered in 2026, and no efficacy results have been published.

paras: It is given by subcutaneous injection and is available only in clinical trials. It is also being tested alongside AZD9550, a GLP-1/glucagon agonist.
Safety is being assessed in phase 1 and phase 3 studies, and no adverse-event data have been published. It is not approved.

angle.text: AZD6234 is AstraZeneca's long-acting amylin agonist injection, followed by fat-loss readers as a fullness-based route to a leaner body. It mimics a satiety hormone to lower appetite and body weight. Phase 3 is registered; no efficacy results are published.

lead: AZD6234 is an investigational long-acting selective amylin receptor agonist developed by AstraZeneca for obesity and type 2 diabetes, given by subcutaneous injection.[1][2] Its connection to appearance is body composition: it is designed to reduce appetite and body weight, which is why it is of interest to people following the next wave of weight-loss injectables after the GLP-1 drugs.

Amylin is a hormone co-secreted with insulin that acts centrally to promote satiety. The first amylin-based drug, pramlintide, found limited use as an add-on to insulin, and longer-acting analogues are now being developed for weight loss.[1][2][3] Efficacy results from AZD6234 trials have not been published; research is at the stage of early-phase studies, with phase 3 trials registered from 2026.[4][5][6]

paras: Amylin is a small peptide hormone that pancreatic beta cells release into the bloodstream with insulin after a meal; it is absent in people with type 1 diabetes.[3] It slows gastric emptying, promotes satiety through hypothalamic receptors distinct from those of GLP-1, and suppresses inappropriate glucagon secretion.[3] Pramlintide (Symlin), developed by Amylin Pharmaceuticals, now an AstraZeneca subsidiary, was approved by the FDA on 16 March 2005 for insulin-using people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, and in trials was associated with reduced HbA1c and weight loss in insulin-treated adults with type 2 diabetes.[3]

A 2026 review calls long-acting amylin analogues a coming class of weight-loss therapy, and a second review summarises experimental data and early-phase trials of amylin analogues across the class.[1][2]

Reviews describe amylin receptors as heterodimers of the calcitonin receptor and receptor activity-modifying proteins, a structure that has guided the design of newer long-acting analogues. Amylin agonists act centrally to induce satiety and slow postprandial glucagon release. [1] A narrative review of amylin analogues for weight loss summarises experimental and early-phase clinical data across the class. [2]

The first-in-human trial, a single-ascending-dose study in healthy participants who are overweight or obese, began in September 2022 with 54 participants, followed by a repeat-dose safety and pharmacokinetic trial that began in November 2023 with 104 participants.[7][8] Further phase 1 work covers renal impairment (24 participants), hepatic impairment of AZD6234 and AZD9550 (28 participants) and relative bioavailability of subcutaneous formulations.[9][10][11][12]

A phase 2 trial combines AZD6234 with AZD9550, a GLP-1/glucagon agonist, for weight loss. The phase 3 programme registered in 2026 spans obesity or overweight without type 2 diabetes (2,500 participants), obesity with type 2 diabetes (1,500), use as an adjunct to incretin-based therapies (500) and a further weight-management study (330) due to start in 2027.[4][5][6][13]

Phase 1 studies have examined single and repeat dosing in overweight or obese participants, renal impairment, hepatic impairment and relative bioavailability of subcutaneous formulations.[8][9][11][7][10][12] AZD6234 is also being tested in combination with AZD9550 in a phase 2 weight-loss trial.

Phase 3 trials registered in 2026 cover obesity or overweight without type 2 diabetes (2,500 participants), obesity with type 2 diabetes (1,500), use as an adjunct to incretin-based therapies (500) and a further weight-management study (330).[4][5][6][13] No efficacy results have been reported.

The compound is a pipeline drug and is discussed mainly in the pharmaceutical and weight-loss-research literature rather than in appearance forums. It has no marketing authorisation anywhere, and access is through trials.[4][5][6]

timeline.event: Pramlintide, the first amylin analogue, approved by the FDA.[3]
Single-ascending-dose phase 1 trial of AZD6234 begins.[7]
Phase 2 combination with AZD9550 and renal impairment study registered.[9]
Phase 3 trials registered in obesity and type 2 diabetes.[4][5][6]
